human_tolerance.notes: 'It is particularly associated with the dry near-desert grasslands of the American southwest, though it is also found in less arid habitats such as pinyon-juniper forest. It is also frequently found in the riparian zones in arid regions' - all three are settings a Colorado street block sits between. It is hunted for sport in Colorado and elsewhere, and competes with the black-tailed jackrabbit for the same diet and habitat.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Year-round breeding: 'Although cottontails are highly active sexually, and mated pairs have multiple litters throughout the year, few young survive to adulthood. Those that survive grow quickly and are full grown at three months.' Timing within the year is set by moisture rather than by season - 'An extremely wet winter season means increased plant life in the spring, and thus increases in cottontail populations' - so no narrower breeding window is claimed.

phases.name: young
phases.note: 'Cottontails give birth to their kits in burrows vacated by other mammals. They sometimes cool off, or take refuge in scratched out shallow created depressions of their own making, using their front paws like a back hoe.' Survival to adulthood is the limiting factor: 'almost every local carnivore larger or faster than the lagomorph is its predator', and snakes 'can catch and eat the young at will; the mother is unable to defend the litter'.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: 'They are not usually active in the middle of the day, but can be observed foraging in the early morning, and early evening. Cottontails are rarely found out of their burrows looking for food on windy days, because the wind interferes with their ability to hear approaching predators.' The phase records the cool-season shelter in burrows and depressions; it is not hibernation, and the fraction is judgement.

external.note: GBIF usage key, authorship and order from the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy; the iNaturalist taxa API matched taxon 43115 to 'Desert Cottontail'; ITIS TSN and NCBI taxon id from Wikidata (P815, P685).

conservation.note: 'Since 1996, the desert cottontail has been rated of least concern on the IUCN Red List; it does not appear on the state or federal list of end...' Wikidata P141 agrees (least concern).

range.note: 'The desert cottontail is found throughout the Western United States from eastern Montana to western Texas, and in Northern and Central Mexico. Its eastern range extends barely into the Great Plains. Westward, its range extends to central Nevada, central and southern California and Baja California, touching the Pacific Ocean. It is found at heights of up to 1,830 m (6,000 ft).' US-CO is included on that basis. The state list is an approximation of that description. NOTE for reviewers: the locale's public centroid sits at about 1,839 m, just above the sourced 1,830 m ceiling, so this species is at the very top of its documented elevational range in Colorado Springs; the elevation_m ceiling is left at the sourced value rather than raised to fit the locale.

traits.note: Covers the structural traits (body plan, limb count, thermoregulation, skin, flight, respiration, metamorphosis) and locomotion modes: the animal 'eats on all fours', uses only its nose to place and turn food on the ground, and escapes 'by hopping away in a zigzag pattern'. hop is the fleeing mode; walk is the slow feeding crawl.

traits.nest_type.note: 'Cottontails give birth to their kits in burrows vacated by other mammals. They sometimes cool off, or take refuge in scratched out shallow created depressions of their own making.' nest_ground carries the shallow scraped depression in habitat.resources.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (~0.95 kg); the validator's size-class bands place this just inside the Small band, immediately below the 1 kg boundary.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of the stated 700-1,200 g range.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Stated range 700 to 1,200 g (1.5 to 2.6 lb).

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of the stated 36-42 cm body length.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'The lifespan of a cottontail that reaches adulthood averages less than two years, depending on the location.' 2.0 years is the upper bound the source gives, taken because the schema asks for a typical figure and the source's only figure is a ceiling.

traits.home_range_ha.note: 'females tend to be larger than the males, but have much smaller home ranges, about 4,000 m2 (1 acre) compared with about 61,000 m2 (15 acres) for a male.' 6.1 ha is the male figure; the female figure is about 0.4 ha. The male value is used because it is the one given as the round number, and the difference is recorded here rather than averaged away.

traits.speed_ms.note: 'Cottontails can reach speeds of over 30 km/h (19 mph)' - a direct conversion of 30 km/h to 8.3 m/s, attached to the hop gait because fleeing is by 'hopping away in a zigzag pattern'. The figure is a floor ('over 30 km/h'), so 8.3 m/s is a lower bound.

traits.diet.note: 'Cottontails are herbivores, with 90% of their diet consisting of grass. They also feed on the leaves and peas of mesquite, barks, fallen fruit, the juicy pads of prickly pear and twigs of shrubs.' The 90% grass share is sourced; the remaining tenth is divided between browse (leaves, twigs, bark) and fruit (fallen fruit and prickly pear pads) as judgement. The source adds that the animal 'rarely needs to drink, getting its water mostly from the plants it eats or from dew' and is coprophagic, re-ingesting its own faeces.

traits.social.note: 'It is social among its peers, often gathering in small groups to feed', and unlike the European rabbit 'they do not form social burrow systems, but compared with some other leporids, they are extremely tolerant of other individuals in their vicinity.' mated pairs have multiple litters, so Pair is not used as the sole structure.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'They are not usually active in the middle of the day, but can be observed foraging in the early morning, and early evening', with reduced activity on windy days because the wind interferes with hearing approaching predators - their primary defence.

traits.defense.note: 'The desert cottontail's normal behavior upon spotting a potential predator is to freeze in place in an attempt to avoid being detected. If it determines that it is in danger, it will flee the area by hopping away in a zigzag pattern.' Freeze is the primary response, with the hop-flee as the backup.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement from the Predators and threats section: it freezes at any disturbance, avoids open ground on windy days, and 'almost every local carnivore larger or faster than the lagomorph is its predator', so a high wariness value was authored even though it habituates to people and lives in settled valleys.

habitat.note: Covers shelter_tag and habitat.resources. Graze, browse and fruit tags come from Diet and feeding; burrow from the birth and refuge sites; nest_ground from the scraped depressions. Weights are judgement, not separately sourced percentages.

habitat.use.note: A terrestrial herbivore throughout: 'the desert cottontail, like all cottontails, eats on all fours', using its nose to move food on the ground and a front paw only to bend a branch; shelter is in burrows and depressions on the ground.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Distribution and habitat and Predators sections: associated with 'the dry near-desert grasslands of the American southwest', also found 'in less arid habitats such as pinyon-juniper forest', 'frequently found in the riparian zones in arid regions' - all three are the settings around a Colorado street block. It is hunted as a game species, and habitat loss from land clearing and cattle grazing 'may severely affect the population'. flight_distance_m is judgement, not a sourced number.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'mated pairs have multiple litters throughout the year' with no migration and no hibernation described, so ActiveYearRound was used.

seasonal.phases.note: Breeding and young-rearing run the whole year in the source, so both phases span 01-01 to 12-31; a cool-season shelter phase is added from the source's statements about daytime inactivity, refuge in burrows and depressions, and foraging only in the early morning and evening. All day-of-month boundaries are judgement because the source gives no dates. The dormancy fraction is judgement: the source says when the animal is hard to see, not what fraction of the population is sheltering, and no hibernation is claimed.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'Those that survive grow quickly and are full grown at three months' - duration_days 90 comes directly from that, with scale 0.35 as judgement for a young animal and requires_tag recording that a burrow must be present, since kits are born in burrows vacated by other mammals. No sourced juvenile-plumage stage is described.

vocalizations.note: HONEST GAP: the record carries an empty vocalizations list, which the schema permits for silent species, because the Desert cottontail article describes no call, grunt or scream anywhere. Lagomorphs of this size are certainly audible; no openly-licensed description was found, so none was invented. fsm-ground-forager-v1 declares no call parameter, so nothing else in the record depends on it.

look.note: Description section: 'The desert cottontail is quite similar in appearance to the European rabbit, though its ears are larger and are more often carried erect', with 'a greyish-brown, rounded tail with a broad white edge and white underside, which is visible as it runs away', and 'white fur on the belly'. The pale belly colour also carries the white tail edge and the white inner ears, since the schema has single slots for each; the ear_ratio is set high because the source stresses the ears are larger than a rabbit's and often carried erect, and the Thermoregulation section adds that 'Ears of desert cottontails make up 14% of their body size'. Proportions are otherwise authored judgement, set from the 36-42 cm length and 7-9 cm hind feet.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program: food_tag is graze, the 90% grass share the program uses for foraging; flee_m 25 reflects the over-30 km/h zigzag hop that carries it out of danger, and flee_gait hop matches that escape; forage_gait walk matches 'eats on all fours'; the rest window 15-88 degrees of sun elevation puts foraging in the early morning and early evening and rest through the middle of the day, matching the source's crepuscular statement.
